Please review the following document.

<document>
Evaluation of the First-Year Peer Mentoring Scheme, 2025-26
Student Success Unit, Northbridge University, July 2026

1. Purpose
Continuation from first to second year is a key regulatory and financial measure for the University. In 2024-25, 13% of full-time first-year undergraduates did not continue into their second year. In 2025-26 the University piloted a peer mentoring scheme for first-year students. This report evaluates the pilot and recommends whether it should be extended.

2. The scheme
Students in their second or third year were recruited and trained as mentors, and each was matched with up to eight first-year mentees from the same faculty. Mentors held a group session every fortnight during the first term and were available for one-to-one meetings throughout the year. Mentors were paid £1,200 for the year. They attended a half-day training session in September covering listening skills, signposting to support services and safeguarding, and were supported by a coordinator in each faculty. First-year students were invited to opt in during welcome week.

Recruiting mentors proved harder than expected. We advertised 200 mentor posts and filled 155, which allowed us to offer places to 1,240 first-year students (155 mentors with eight mentees each). Mentee places were taken up within the first two weeks and a waiting list was closed at 300 names.

3. Who took part
Of the 4,100 full-time first-year students, 1,240 took part. Mentees were more likely than other first-years to be living in university halls (78% compared with 52%) and were somewhat more likely to have entered with higher tariff qualifications. They were similar to non-mentees in age and gender.

4. Results
Table 1. Continuation into second year, 2025-26 entrants
Group | Students | Continuing to year two | Continuation rate
Mentored | 1,240 | 1,166 | 94.0%
Not mentored | 2,860 | 2,460 | 86.0%
All first-years | 4,100 | 3,626 | 88.4%

Mentored students were eight percentage points more likely to continue into their second year. Overall continuation rose to 88.4%, from 87% the previous year.

The eight-point gap is clear evidence that peer mentoring improves continuation. Applied to the 1,240 mentees, it means that around 99 students continued who would otherwise have left. At £9,250 a year in tuition fee income, these students are worth about £1.2 million to the University in their second year alone.

Mentees rated the scheme 4.3 out of 5 in the end-of-year survey, and many commented that it helped them settle in and find out about support services. Mentors reported that the role improved their own confidence and employability.

5. Costs
The pilot cost £186,000 for mentor pay, £12,000 for training and £18,000 for coordination, a total of £216,000, or about £174 per mentee.

6. Recommendation
We recommend that from 2026-27 peer mentoring becomes a standard part of the first-year experience, with every full-time first-year student allocated a mentor automatically rather than opting in. On the pilot's costs of about £174 per mentee, this would cost around £714,000 a year for 4,100 students. On the pilot's results, it would raise continuation to around 94% across the whole first-year cohort, a gain of over 200 continuing students a year, and the fee income retained would cover the cost several times over.

7. Conclusion
The pilot has shown that peer mentoring improves continuation by eight percentage points, pays for itself many times over, and is valued by mentees and mentors alike. Extending it to all first-year students is a clear opportunity to improve outcomes and secure the University's continuation performance.
</document>
response:
# Review: Evaluation of the First-Year Peer Mentoring Scheme, 2025-26

## Overall assessment

The report is clearly written, and most of its figures check out. But its central claim, that mentoring caused the eight-point continuation gap, is not supported by the evidence. The recommendation and the financial case depend entirely on that claim. One financial figure is also wrong. The scheme may well be worthwhile, but the report overstates what the pilot shows, and the recommendation goes further than the evidence allows.

## Major issues

### 1. The eight-point gap is not evidence of causation

Students opted in, so mentees and non-mentees differ in ways that predict continuation regardless of mentoring:

- **Accommodation:** 78% of mentees lived in halls, compared with 52% of non-mentees. Living in halls is a well-known predictor of continuation.
- **Entry qualifications:** mentees had higher tariff qualifications, another strong predictor.
- **Motivation:** places filled within two weeks of welcome week. The students who signed up quickly are likely the more engaged and better-integrated ones, which the report does not measure.

The report itself shows these differences (Section 3) but never accounts for them. Some or all of the gap could be explained by who chose to take part. Statements such as "clear evidence that peer mentoring improves continuation" (Section 4) and "has shown that peer mentoring improves continuation by eight percentage points" (Section 7) are not justified.

### 2. The report's own figures suggest the effect is much smaller

- If mentoring had caused around 99 extra students to continue, overall continuation should have risen by about 2.4 points (99 ÷ 4,100). It actually rose by 1.4 points, from 87% to 88.4%, or about 57 students. Even that rise is not attributable to the scheme without controlling for differences between cohorts.
- Non-mentees continued at 86.0%, below the previous year's whole-cohort rate of 87%. This is what you would expect if the scheme mainly sorted stronger students into the mentored group and left a weaker remainder, rather than improving outcomes overall.

### 3. Arithmetic error in the financial benefit

99 students × £9,250 = **£915,750**, not "about £1.2 million". £1.2 million would require about 130 students. This needs correcting, and in any case it rests on the causal assumption in issue 1.

### 4. The scale-up projection does not follow from the pilot

The recommendation assumes that every first-year student would reach the mentees' 94% rate. That assumption has several problems:

- **It takes the whole gap as causal** (see issue 1).
- **It changes the population.** The recommendation moves from opt-in to automatic allocation. Pilot mentees were self-selected volunteers. Students allocated a mentor without choosing one are likely to engage less, and they include the students most at risk of leaving. Their results cannot be assumed to match the volunteers'.
- **Recruiting mentors is a serious constraint.** Covering 4,100 students at eight mentees each needs about 513 mentors, 3.3 times the 155 recruited in the pilot. The pilot also failed to fill its 200 advertised posts. The report does not say how this would be achieved. Higher pay or larger groups would change both the cost and possibly the effect.
- **The cost per mentee assumes full groups.** The £174 figure only holds if every mentor has eight mentees. Coordination costs may not scale linearly either.

### 5. Timing and definition of "continuation"

The report is dated July 2026. At that point, 2025-26 entrants could not yet have continued into their second year. The standard continuation measure (e.g. the OfS definition) is assessed around a year and two weeks after the student started. The report should say how continuation was measured: progression decisions, re-enrolment intentions, or something else. It should also note that the figures were provisional. Since final figures should now be available, the analysis should be updated with them.

## Minor issues

- **Survey results:** the 4.3/5 rating needs a response rate. Only students who stayed to the end of the year were surveyed, so those who left are missing. Mentor-reported benefits to their own confidence and employability are self-reported and unmeasured.
- **Participation:** there is no information on how many mentees actually attended group sessions or one-to-one meetings. A dose-response analysis comparing active and nominal mentees would be informative, though it would still be subject to selection.
- **Revenue vs. benefit:** £9,250 is tuition income, not net benefit. It also applies only to home students (international fees differ), and retained students carry teaching costs. The figure also ignores whether retained students go on to complete their degrees.
- **Faculty mix:** mentors were matched within faculties, and mentee faculty composition is not reported. Continuation rates vary by subject.
- **Consistency of the multiplier:** Section 6 says "several times over" and Section 7 says "many times over". These should be harmonised once the figures are corrected.

## Suggested improvements to the analysis

1. **Use the waiting list.** The 300 students who wanted a place but did not get one are a much better comparison group than all non-mentees, because they share the motivation to sign up. Their continuation rate is the single most useful figure the report could add.
2. **Adjust for known predictors.** Compare outcomes within groups (halls vs. not, tariff bands, faculty, and ideally widening-participation markers), or use regression or matching. Report the adjusted gap alongside the raw one.
3. **Present a range of scenarios.** Show the financial case under several assumed effect sizes, e.g. 1, 2.5 and 8 points. Even a modest effect may cover £714,000: about 77 extra continuing students would break even on first-year fee income alone, roughly a 1.9-point effect across 4,100 students.
4. **Revise the recommendation.** Demand exceeded supply in the pilot, so there is a natural opportunity to allocate places by lottery among applicants next year, or to roll the scheme out faculty by faculty. Either would give a credible estimate of the effect before committing £714,000 a year. The opt-out model could also be trialled in a subset of faculties to test whether non-volunteers benefit.
5. **Address mentor recruitment** explicitly before any scale-up.

## Corrected or checked figures

| Item | Report | Check |
|---|---|---|
| Mentored continuation rate | 94.0% | 1,166/1,240 = 94.0% ✓ |
| Non-mentored continuation rate | 86.0% | 2,460/2,860 = 86.0% ✓ |
| Overall continuation rate | 88.4% | 3,626/4,100 = 88.4% ✓ |
| Mentor pay | £186,000 | 155 × £1,200 ✓ |
| Cost per mentee | ~£174 | £216,000/1,240 = £174.19 ✓ |
| Full rollout cost | ~£714,000 | £174.19 × 4,100 = £714,194 ✓ |
| Fee value of 99 students | ~£1.2m | **£915,750** ✗ |
| Mentors needed for full rollout | not stated | ~513 (vs. 155 recruited) |

## Bottom line

The pilot is promising and popular, and the case for continuing it is reasonable. The evidence does not yet support the claim of an eight-point causal effect or the projected whole-cohort rate of 94%. I'd recommend reframing the conclusion as "promising but unproven", correcting the £1.2m figure, adding the waiting-list comparison and adjusted analysis, and changing the recommendation to a further year with randomised or phased allocation rather than an immediate universal opt-out rollout.
